topics.name: Rational numbers
topics.kicker: Fractions of integers · Decimals that end or repeat
topics.dates: Egyptian fractions in the Rhind Papyrus, c. 1550 BCE
topics.briefing: A rational number is any number that can be written as a fraction of two integers, like ½, −7/3, or 5 (which is 5/1); the name comes from the word “ratio.” As decimals, rational numbers either stop, like 0.75, or repeat forever, like 0.333…. Numbers such as √2 and π can’t be written as fractions, and a legend says the ancient Greek Hippasus was punished for revealing that √2 is not rational.
topics.answerHtml: rational numbers (accept rationals; prompt on Q or fractions; do not accept “irrational numbers” or “real numbers”)

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: According to legend, the Pythagorean Hippasus [“HIP-uh-sus”] was drowned at sea after revealing that the diagonal of a square with side 1 is not one of these numbers. The classic proof of that fact assumes the diagonal is one of them in lowest terms, then shows that its top and bottom would both have to be even.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, such as one-half and negative 3, that can be written as a fraction of two integers.

tossups.p: The Calkin–Wilf tree, described in 2000, lists every positive one of these numbers exactly once, which shows that they can be counted. Georg Cantor proved that there are exactly as many of these numbers as there are counting numbers, even though infinitely many of them lie between any two whole numbers.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, which can be written as one integer divided by another nonzero integer.

tossups.p: Giuseppe Peano [“pay-AH-noh”] chose a letter for the set of these numbers in 1895, taking it from the Italian word for “quotient.” In lowest terms, one of these numbers has a decimal that stops exactly when its denominator has no prime factors other than 2 and 5.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, written with a double-struck Q, whose decimals either end or repeat.

tossups.p: Egyptian scribes, as in the Rhind [“RYND”] Papyrus, wrote positive numbers of this kind as sums of different unit fractions, and Fibonacci’s _Liber Abaci_ gave a method in 1202 that always works. One-seventh, written as a decimal, repeats the block 142857 forever.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, such as two-fifths, that can be written as a fraction of two integers.

tossups.p: A theorem says that if a polynomial with integer coefficients has a root of this type, written p over q in lowest terms, then p divides the constant term and q divides the leading coefficient. That test shows that x squared minus 2 has no roots of this type.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers that can be written as fractions of integers, whose decimals end or repeat.

tossups.p: Thomae’s [“TOH-mayz”] “popcorn function” is continuous at every point except these numbers. The Dirichlet [“deer-ih-KLAY”] function equals 1 at each of these numbers and 0 everywhere else, so it is continuous nowhere, since every interval contains both kinds of points.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, like three-fourths, that can be written as a fraction of two integers.

tossups.p: In 1978, Roger Apéry [“ah-pay-REE”] proved that the sum of the reciprocals of the perfect cubes is not one of these numbers. Johann Heinrich Lambert had proved in 1761 that pi is not one of these numbers either, so it can’t be written exactly as a fraction like 22 over 7.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, which are quotients of two integers and whose decimals either end or repeat forever.

tossups.p: Lester Ford drew a circle touching the number line at each of these numbers, and no two of his circles ever cross. John Farey’s sequences list these numbers between 0 and 1 in order of size, using only denominators up to a fixed limit.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers that can be written as one integer over another.

tossups.p: These are exactly the numbers whose continued fractions come to an end, while the continued fraction for phi, about 1.618, is made of 1s forever. Between any two of these numbers lies another one, such as their average.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, written with a double-struck Q, that include every integer and every fraction.

tossups.p: Although these numbers are crowded densely along the number line, together they take up zero total length, so almost every number on the line is not one of them. Richard Dedekind [“DAY-duh-kint”] defined the real numbers in 1872 by cutting the set of these numbers into two pieces.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, such as five-eighths, that can be written as a fraction of two integers.

tossups.p: Points on the unit circle whose coordinates are both numbers of this kind, such as three-fifths and four-fifths, correspond to Pythagorean triples like 3, 4, 5. Adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing two of these numbers, except dividing by zero, always gives another one.
tossups.r: Every integer is one, since 5 equals 5 over 1. For 10 points, name these numbers that can be written as fractions.

tossups.p: Archimedes’ estimate 22 over 7 and Zu Chongzhi’s [“zoo chong-JUR”] even closer estimate 355 over 113 are numbers of this kind that approximate pi. Writing one of these numbers in lowest terms means dividing its top and bottom by their greatest common divisor.
tossups.r: Any repeating decimal, like 0.0909 repeating, which equals one-eleventh, is one of these. For 10 points, name these numbers that can be written as a quotient of two integers.

tossups.p: Multiplying 0.2727 repeating by 100 and then subtracting the original decimal shows that it equals 27 over 99, or 3 over 11, so it is one of these numbers. Between any two of these numbers lies another, so none of them has a “next” one.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, which can be written as fractions of integers and include all the integers.

tossups.p: The square root of a whole number is one of these numbers only if that whole number is a perfect square, so the square roots of 2, 3, and 5 are not. Leonhard Euler showed that the number e, about 2.718, is not one of these numbers either.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers that can be written as fractions of integers, whose decimals end or repeat.

tossups.p: In Pythagorean tuning, the octave and the perfect fifth come from string lengths in the proportions 2 to 1 and 3 to 2, both numbers of this kind. Dividing any one of these numbers by another nonzero one always gives a number of this kind.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name these numbers, like three-halves, that can be written as a fraction of two integers.

clues.t: Numbers that can be written as a fraction p/q of two integers, with q not 0; in lowest terms, the top and bottom share no common factor
Their decimals either end (0.75) or repeat forever (0.333…)
Written with a double-struck Q (ℚ), for “quotient”
Every integer is one (5 = 5/1), but √2 and π are not
Legend says the Pythagorean Hippasus was drowned at sea for revealing that √2, the diagonal of a square with side 1, is not one of these
Georg Cantor showed they can be listed one by one, so there are exactly as many of them as counting numbers
Between any two lies another (such as their average), yet they leave gaps like √2; Dedekind’s 1872 cuts filled the gaps to make the real numbers
Adding, subtracting, multiplying, or dividing (except by 0) two of them always gives another one
In lowest terms, its decimal ends exactly when the denominator has no prime factors but 2 and 5; otherwise it repeats, like 1/7 = 0.142857142857…
Egyptians, as in the Rhind Papyrus, wrote positive ones as sums of different unit fractions; Fibonacci’s _Liber Abaci_ (1202) gave a method that always works
If a polynomial with integer coefficients has a root p/q of this kind in lowest terms, p divides the constant term and q divides the leading coefficient
Every repeating decimal is one: 0.0909… is 1/11, 0.2727… is 27/99 = 3/11 (multiply by 100 and subtract), and 0.999… is exactly 1
The square root of a whole number is one only if that number is a perfect square; Leonhard Euler showed e is not one
Giuseppe Peano chose their letter in 1895 from the Italian word for “quotient”
Roger Apéry proved in 1978 that the sum of the reciprocals of the cubes (1 + 1/8 + 1/27 + …) is not one
Johann Heinrich Lambert proved in 1761 that π is not one, so 22/7 is only an estimate
Thomae’s popcorn function is continuous everywhere except at these; the Dirichlet function is 1 at these and 0 elsewhere, so it is continuous nowhere
Farey sequences list them between 0 and 1 in order, with denominators up to a limit; Ford circles touch the number line at each one and never cross
Exactly these numbers have continued fractions that end; the continued fraction for φ (phi, about 1.618) is all 1s forever
The Calkin–Wilf tree (2000) lists every positive one exactly once, which shows that they can be counted
Though crowded everywhere on the number line, they take up zero total length, so almost every number on the line is not one
The classic proof that √2 is not one assumes it is a fraction in lowest terms and shows its top and bottom would both be even, a contradiction
Points of this kind on the unit circle, like (3/5, 4/5), match Pythagorean triples such as 3, 4, 5
Archimedes’ 22/7 and Zu Chongzhi’s 355/113 are numbers of this kind that approximate π
Pythagorean tuning builds the octave and the perfect fifth from string lengths in the proportions 2 to 1 and 3 to 2

trap.title: Rational or irrational?
trap.body: Rational numbers (fractions p/q, or decimals that end or repeat) and irrational numbers (like √2, π, and e, whose decimals never end or repeat) are opposite answer lines, and together they make up the real numbers. A tossup about the Pythagoreans and √2 may want either one, depending on whether it says √2 is “not one of these” or “one of these.”
trap.fix: Listen to the wording: “√2 is not one of these” or “a fraction of two integers” means rational numbers; “√2 and π are examples” means irrational numbers; clues that include both kinds, or the whole number line, mean real numbers. Saying only “fractions” earns a prompt.
trap.line: Real answer line: rational numbers (accept rationals; prompt on Q or fractions; do not accept “irrational numbers” or “real numbers”)

topics.name: The number two
topics.kicker: The only even prime · The base of the binary system
topics.briefing: Two is the smallest prime number and the only even one, since every other even number can be divided by 2. It is the base of binary, the 0-and-1 system computers use, and its square root, about 1.414, is the length of the diagonal of a square with sides of 1. Legend says the Pythagoreans were so upset to learn that √2 can’t be written as a fraction that they punished the man who revealed it.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: The Babylonian clay tablet YBC 7289 shows the square root of this number, the length of the diagonal of a square with side 1, correct to five decimal places. Legend says the Pythagorean Hippasus [“HIP-uh-sus”] was drowned at sea for revealing that the square root of this number cannot be written as a fraction.
tossups.r: Its square root is about 1.414. For 10 points, name this smallest prime number, the only prime that is even.

tossups.p: Alfred North Whitehead and Bertrand Russell’s _Principia Mathematica_ took hundreds of pages to prove that 1 plus 1 equals this number. Aristotle wrote that, strictly speaking, this is the smallest number, since many Greek thinkers did not count 1 as a number at all.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, the base of the binary system, which uses only the digits 0 and 1.

tossups.p: Christian Goldbach’s still-unproven conjecture says that every even number greater than this number is the sum of this many primes. Primes such as 11 and 13, which differ by this number, are believed to go on forever.
tossups.r: Such primes are called twin primes. For 10 points, name this only even prime number.

tossups.p: In 2024, the volunteer project GIMPS found a prime with more than 41 million digits that is 1 less than a power of this number. Primes of that form, named for Marin Mersenne [“mair-SEN”], require the exponent to be prime as well.
tossups.r: Every even number is divisible by this number. For 10 points, name this number, the base of the binary system.

tossups.p: Leonhard Euler showed that for any convex polyhedron, the number of vertices minus the number of edges plus the number of faces equals this number. A cube, for example, gives 8 minus 12 plus 6.
tossups.r: Each U.S. state elects this many senators. For 10 points, name this number, which equals 1 plus 1 and is the smallest prime.

tossups.p: Andrew Wiles proved in the 1990s that a to the n plus b to the n equals c to the n has no solutions in positive whole numbers when n is greater than this number. The Pythagorean theorem raises each side of a right triangle to this power.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, the only even prime, which is also the base of the binary system.

tossups.p: Newton’s law of gravitation and Coulomb’s law each say that a force weakens with the distance raised to this power. In Albert Einstein’s equation relating mass and energy, the speed of light is raised to this power.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, which is the smallest prime number and the only even one.

tossups.p: Each atomic orbital can hold at most this many electrons, which must have opposite spins under the Pauli exclusion principle. Helium, the noble gas right after hydrogen, has this atomic number, and each molecule of hydrogen gas contains this many atoms.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, the smallest prime and the base of the binary system.

tossups.p: In 1703, Gottfried Leibniz [“LYBE-nits”] published a paper on a number system based on this number, comparing it to the broken and solid lines of the Chinese _I Ching_. In that system, the number 5 is written 101.
tossups.r: That system, binary, uses only the digits 0 and 1. For 10 points, name this number, the only even prime.

tossups.p: Sheets of A4 paper have sides in proportion to the square root of this number, so folding one so its short edges meet makes a smaller sheet of the same shape. That square root, about 1.414, may have been the first number shown to be irrational.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, which equals 1 plus 1 and is the only even prime number.

tossups.p: The points of a graph can be colored with just this many colors, so that no line joins points of the same color, exactly when the graph has no loops of odd length. In classical logic, every statement has one of this many truth values.
tossups.r: A chessboard’s squares need only this many colors. For 10 points, name this number, the smallest prime.

tossups.p: The natural logarithm of this number, about 0.693, equals the sum of the alternating harmonic series. Money growing at 1 percent interest per year takes about 70 years to grow to this many times its starting amount.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, the only even prime, which is written 10 in binary.

tossups.p: By the fundamental theorem of algebra, which Carl Friedrich Gauss proved in his 1799 thesis, every quadratic polynomial has exactly this many complex roots, counting repeats. When a quadratic’s discriminant is positive, its parabola crosses the x-axis this many times.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, the degree of a quadratic equation and the smallest prime.

tossups.p: Euclid’s first postulate says that any set of this many points can be joined by a straight line. Leonhard Euler showed that 1 plus one-fourth plus one-ninth plus one-sixteenth, and so on forever, equals pi raised to this power, divided by 6.
tossups.r: A circle’s diameter is this many times its radius. For 10 points, name this number, the smallest prime number.

tossups.p: Leonhard Euler showed in 1736 that a walk crossing every bridge exactly once is possible only if zero or this many land areas touch an odd number of bridges, which ruled out such a walk in Königsberg. This number to the tenth power is 1,024.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this number, the only even prime number, which is the base of the binary system.

clues.t: The only even prime number, and the smallest prime of all
The base of the binary number system, which uses only the digits 0 and 1; in binary it is written 10
1 + 1 equals it, and every even number is divisible by it
It plus itself, it times itself, and it raised to its own power all equal 4
Its square root, about 1.414, is the diagonal of a square with side 1 and may have been the first number shown to be irrational
Goldbach’s conjecture: every even number greater than it is a sum of this many primes; twin primes, like 11 and 13, differ by it
Euler’s polyhedron formula: vertices − edges + faces equals it for any convex polyhedron (cube: 8 − 12 + 6)
Fermat’s Last Theorem: aⁿ + bⁿ = cⁿ has no positive whole-number solutions for n greater than it, the exponent in the Pythagorean theorem
Gravity and Coulomb’s law weaken with the distance raised to this power, and Einstein’s mass–energy equation raises the speed of light to it
Helium’s atomic number; each atomic orbital holds at most this many electrons, with opposite spins (the Pauli exclusion principle)
Mersenne primes are 1 less than a power of it, with a prime exponent; in 2024, GIMPS found one with more than 41 million digits
Quadratic equations have this degree, so they have this many complex roots counting repeats; a positive discriminant means the parabola crosses the x-axis this many times
Gottfried Leibniz’s 1703 paper on the number system based on it compared that system to the broken and solid lines of the _I Ching_
A circle’s diameter is this many times its radius (circumference = this number × π × radius); each U.S. state elects this many senators
The Babylonian tablet YBC 7289 shows its square root correct to five decimal places (1.41421)
Legend says the Pythagorean Hippasus was drowned at sea for revealing that its square root cannot be written as a fraction
Whitehead and Russell’s _Principia Mathematica_ took hundreds of pages to prove that 1 + 1 equals it
Aristotle wrote that, strictly speaking, it is the smallest number, since many Greek thinkers did not count 1 as a number
A4 paper’s sides are in proportion to its square root, so folding a sheet so its short edges meet gives a smaller sheet of the same shape
A graph can be colored with this many colors exactly when it has no loops of odd length; a chessboard needs only this many, and classical logic has this many truth values
Its natural logarithm, about 0.693, is the sum of the alternating harmonic series; at 1% interest, money takes about 70 years to grow to this many times its size
Euler (1736): a walk crossing every bridge once needs zero or this many land areas touching an odd number of bridges, which ruled out Königsberg
It raised to the tenth power is 1,024, close to a thousand
Euler’s Basel problem: 1 + 1/4 + 1/9 + 1/16 + … equals π raised to this power, divided by 6
Euclid’s first postulate: any set of this many points can be joined by a straight line

trap.title: The number, not binary
trap.body: Clues about this number often name things built on it: binary numbers (base 2), the square root of 2, prime numbers, or twin primes. Those are separate answer lines, so answering “binary” or “prime” when the question asks for “this number” is wrong. And “1 + 1” clues say 1 out loud but want the result, 2.
trap.fix: When you hear “only even prime,” “base of binary,” “its square root is about 1.414,” or “Goldbach,” say “two.” If the question asks for “this number system,” say binary; if it asks for “these numbers” with exactly two factors, say prime numbers.
